title: Rust 1.100
author: mbStavola
relevanceReason: 命中 3 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.100.0 with: $ rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0. If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across!
Never type Allocator API DropGuard API Conjuring zero-sized types Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo min-publish-age Stabilized APIs

Never type After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable! This also completes the project goal for this work. The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return, break, and std::process::exit, also have the type !. Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if: fn mrrrow(option: Option<u32>) { let value = match option { // `x` has type `u32` Some(x) => x, // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`, // allowing the `match` to pass type checking. None => return, }; // ... } While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions (-> !), this release allows naming the never type anywhere: fn infallible_unwrap<T>(res: Result<T, !>) -> T { // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before let Ok(v) = res; v } Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using !. This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization). Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible, we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable. We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.

Allocator API This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api, enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box. These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait. This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!

comments.author: nirinor
comments.textRawHtml:
Woohoo, that's a release! My personal favorites:

- Stabilize never type

- Stabilize custom allocators

- Introduced minimum publish age configurations, also known as dependency cooldowns. When the relevant config is set, the resolver ignores versions published more recently than that, unless they are already in Cargo.lock. (RFC 3923) docs #17335

- cargo-install: now uses the existing lockfile in the .crate tarball by default. --locked in cargo install becomes a no-op. #17388

children.author: SOLAR_FIELDS
children.textRawHtml:
Dependency cooldowns receiving such a whiplash this year. Earlier everyone was advocating for them because of the supply chain attacks. Now, people are worried because you might miss 0 days if you use them.

Nonetheless, the ability to set and configure it is a welcome feature.

children.author: woodruffw
children.textRawHtml:
You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down, and you should immediately patch security advisories.

One of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.

children.author: kragen
children.textRawHtml:
Usually people advocate dependency cooldowns as a mitigation for supply-chain attacks, where you're depending on a module with a malicious maintainer, possibly a new one (perhaps one who stole the old maintainer's keys so they can pretend to be the old maintainer).

In that situation, how do you distinguish between "normal updates" (that you should let cool down) and "security advisories"? If all the hypothetical malicious maintainer has to do to get you to update is to publish a security advisory for their own package, wouldn't they just do that? It might even be a real advisory about a real security hole that they introduced, but claiming more versions are affected than actually are affected.

children.author: woodruffw
children.textRawHtml: It takes additional permissions, in general, to issue an advisory. And “supply chain” attacks in general tend to be used by smash-and-grab attackers, who don’t have time on their side. It’s not like a browser 0day where the attacker’s goal is to preserve their underlying exploit primitive for as long as possible.

children.author: ninkendo
children.textRawHtml:
How do you separate security advisories from regular updates? (If it’s just a box you check, it only means attackers will say “this is a security update” on the malicious package they upload.)

The point of cooldowns is for when a crate author’s account is compromised and used to publish malicious code. Saying “security advisories bypass cooldowns” wouldn’t really help anything there.

But I guess an alternative could be to update using the cooldown, and then diff the dependencies that would get a newer version if the cooldown wasn't in place to check if they contain anything relevant for the particular application you're developing.

children.author: derefr
children.textRawHtml:
Why wouldn't a supply-chain attacker simply manipulate the project into producing a security advisory to get their exploit code pushed through inside a high-priority release?

I.e. get a puppet/co-conspirator to push vulnerable code; wait until that code gets released as v1.2.3; submit other vulnerable code; wait for that code to be merged and released as v1.2.4; then submit a vuln report for the vuln introduced in v1.2.3; and wait for v1.2.3 + v1.2.4 to be security-deprecated and v1.2.5 to be fast-released to replace them.

Now v1.2.5 exists and has your still-unknown 0day in it, while versions prior to v1.2.5 are deprecated. If devtools that had pinned v1.2.3 get forced "upward" to v1.2.5 despite the cooldown, you win.

children.author: dns_snek
children.textRawHtml:
I haven't seen anyone advocate against cooldowns because those are completely different problems.

How would removing cooldowns help you patch vulnerabilities? That would imply that your CI is configured to update dependencies, rebuild, and push them to production without human oversight?

That's obviously not the way to go, you must have human oversight and if you do then your humans should be alerted when one of your dependencies patches a security issue. At that point you review it, override the cooldown, and push it to production.

children.textRawHtml: You should use a cooldown. The effects of a supply chain attack are significantly worse than the effects of a 0 day. You can always make exceptions on a case-by-case basis.
